title: AI won’t replace biologists — it’ll just join the staff
excerpt: Everyone wants to know if AI will replace their job. Jennifer Doudna, co-inventor of CRISPR, has a clear-eyed take from inside the lab.
content_html:
Jennifer Doudna, Nobel Prize winner, biochemist, and CRISPR co-inventor, breaks down how AI is already reshaping experimental biology: speeding up mundane tasks like data cleanup and formatting, and increasingly helping spot patterns in large datasets that would be nearly impossible to catch by hand. But Doudna draws a clear line — AI agents can execute a protocol, not design one, and they still can't make the on-the-fly judgment calls a researcher makes in the lab every day. Her take on the future isn't scientists replaced by robots, but scientists working alongside AI coworkers who handle the grunt work, freeing humans to ask the harder questions.

JENNIFER DOUDNA: There's a lot of discussion about AI and biology, a lot, right? And people are always asking me about this too. You know, how is AI going to change biology? How is it going to change the genome editing?

And my immediate answer is, well, it's certainly going to accelerate everything. It's making our work go a lot faster because we can increasingly speed up things that used to take a lot more time. And I think in the future that'll happen even more. You know, I do imagine a day when we can use AI to help us predict which experiments are going to be worth doing. And that means that we don't have to do as many, we hope, you know. But I think artificial intelligence absolutely needs human intelligence in biology to be useful.

Scientists are increasingly using AI in biology to accelerate the rate of experimentation. And the way they're doing this is in a few ways. They are using it to do very, you know, kind of mundane types of things that we used to have to spend a lot of time on. And I'm referring here to things like writing summaries of projects that we need to submit, you know, taking large data sets and culling them, organizing data into different domains, combining different types of sets of data, converting data from one format into another. All those types of things used to take huge amounts of time. Sometimes they still do. But, you know, increasingly, AI is a real assist there. So that's very interesting. And lots of people are using it now for that kind of thing.

What I think is potentially more interesting, but is going to take longer, but we're starting to see this happening, is that scientists are using AI to make predictions about data, to discover things in sets of data that might be very hard to discern manually, but where a machine learning system can go through data and find trends that would be hard to see by inspecting data yourself, but a machine system that has the ability to look across large sets of data for small but significant trends can pick these out. I think that's very exciting. And we're seeing this happening more and more.

And I do think in the future, as scientists become better at applying AI to particular questions in biology, that we're going to see an acceleration of even things like hypothesis generation and the ability to answer questions that might have taken a long time previously, but can go fast now because you can use coding agents, for example, to write code quickly. So those are where I'm seeing really interesting opportunities even now, and it's going to accelerate in the future.

In experimental biology, it's interesting to think about the role of computation. I think, you know, when I started out in biology, we used computers to do things that were, you know, annoying, but, you know, needed to get done and were very hard to do manually. And I'm thinking about things like converting data from one format to another, combining sets of data together. You know, I used to be focusing on molecular structure determination using X-ray crystallography, for example. And that was a field where at the time we did lots of, you know, collecting of X-ray diffraction data from crystals and then combining data from different crystals, having to convert it into different formats, things of that type, even just collating data, you know, things that sound very boring, and they were, but they had to be done and they had to be done right. So we used computation that way back in those days. But, you know, increasingly, you know, computers and the models that we're training on data sets are becoming a lot more sophisticated. So increasingly, we're able to use these for predictions and for the kinds of, you know, accelerations of experimental science that weren't possible in the past.

Do I think scientists will become, you know, desk jockeys in the future? No. And the reason is that I don't see robots — you know, this would require really very sophisticated robots. And I think that robotics right now, even with some of the exciting things that have happened, just are not at the point, and frankly, probably not even close to being capable the way a person is to make changes to experiments on the fly. We do this all the time in the lab. It's kind of a natural thing for a graduate student or a postdoc in the lab to be working on a protocol and realize that, oh, I need to double the volume of this thing, or I need to change the way I'm doing some manipulation of a sample. That's something that a person can do easily on the fly, whereas for a machine, it would take a lot of effort. And believe me, I've seen this myself in my lab, how much work it is to change a robotic format that we have for a robot versus just telling a student, hey, you know, instead of, you know, manipulating the sample this way, do it that way. They can change like that.

What I think is going to happen in the future with experimental science is actually that I think each person who is an experimentalist, like, let's say, a graduate student, will effectively have a set of technical staff that are computers or AI agents assisting them. And those AI agents will be brilliant, but somewhat naive about the actual details of the project. And so we find this now, you know, that students are using particularly coding agents this way, where they have coding agents that are set up to help with data manipulation, help them with collecting data in an experiment, even designing how to collect the data. But they don't have the ability to tell the scientist, this is the experiment you should be doing, or you should be doing it this way and not that way, depending, again, sort of depending on the details. But this is really what we're seeing.

And so I imagine that will probably be true for a while, again, because it gets back to this knowledge of how do we ever get enough data to train models to be able to not only kind of regurgitate things that they've been trained on, but to really be innovative and come up with new ideas. I don't see that in the near future.
